1.pericope_label: Two thousand cubits behind the ark: sanctify yourselves

schools.summary: Supply the structure rather than the detail. The crossing is narrated in two chapters and falls into three parts — the commencement, the further progress, and the close — and in each the command of God to Joshua is mentioned first, then its communication to the people, and finally its execution. Note what that arrangement implies: Joshua's issuing these commands with a prediction of the miracle presupposes that the Lord had already made his will known to him, which confirms the conclusions drawn about how the materials are ordered.

Fix the day by the Jewish calendar, since the reckoning can be carried through: Moses died on the seventh of Adar, the thirty days of mourning for him ended on the seventh of Nisan, the spies were sent two days before they were ended and returned on the eighth, so the morning on which Joshua rose early was the ninth, and the crossing fell on the tenth. Or reckon instead from the announcement rather than the departure, three days after it had been intimated, since they did not halt at the bank longer than one night; and note that although the form of the miracle is not yet explained, when the ark of the covenant is brought forward like a banner to guide the way it was natural to infer that the Lord was preparing something unusual. Their faith is proved by the suspense, for it was an example of rare virtue to obey and follow the ark while uninformed as to the result — and this is the special characteristic of faith, not to inquire curiously what the Lord is to do, nor dispute subtly how what he declares can possibly be done, but to cast all our anxious cares upon his providence. On the distance from the ark, declare its dignity by the interval, recalling what happened to Uzzah when with inconsiderate zeal he put forth his hand to support it; and add a reason beyond reverence, that the distance exercised their faith by keeping them from confining the grace of God within narrow limits, reminding them that though far from the ark his power was ever near. Also notice the marginal reading, between you and them, and dispose of what grew out of it — a Jewish fiction of two arks travelling together, that of the divine Majesty and that holding Joseph's bones, which the rabbis notice but which has no foundation in the text.

Take the three days as the spies' own errand, so that they returned on the third day and the proclamation followed at once, the people striking their tents and marching to Jordan; and add a dating from Usher, the twenty-eighth of April in the fortieth year after the exodus, with the distance from Shittim to Jordan given from Josephus as about eight English miles. On the ark's new station, hold that till this time it went in the middle of the cloudy pillar and now goes in front, the pillar of fire and cloud probably still hovering over it. On the two thousand cubits, give two plain reasons: the greater respect due to what was the symbol and pledge of the divine presence, and that the ark, which was to be their pilot over these waters, might be the more conspicuous, which it could not have been had the people crowded upon it. On sanctifying themselves, suppose the command implied what Moses had required at Sinai, that they wash themselves and their garments and abstain from everything which might indispose their minds from a profitable attention to the miracle; and ask it of soul and body both, that they might be meet to receive such a favour. And on the priests bearing the ark, call it remarkable that this fell to them and not to the Levites whose ordinary business it was, report the conjecture that the ark was carried uncovered here and not wrapped in its curtains as the Levites carried it, and list the other occasions when priests alone performed the office — while stating the rule simply, that although the Levites were to carry the ark the priests might perform that office and did so on some solemn occasions.

Be interested not in the arithmetic but in the marching. Though they were not yet told how they should pass the river, and were unprovided for passing it in any ordinary way, they went forward in faith, having been told that they should pass it; and we must go on in the way of our duty though we foresee difficulties, trusting God to help us through them when we come to them. Let us proceed as far as we can, and depend on divine sufficiency for that which we find ourselves not sufficient for. Make the early rising a note of character, intimating how little Joshua loved his ease and how much his business: those that would bring great things to pass must rise early. Then take the pillar as removed, since otherwise it would have led them — unless we suppose it now hovered over the ark and they had a double guide. Note also the change of station: formerly the ark was carried in the midst of the camp, but now it went before them to search out a resting-place and, as it were, to put them in possession of the promised land. And say what following it means: they must remove and go after it as those resolved never to forsake it, for wherever God's ordinances are, there we must be.

debates.question: What are the three days of verse 2?

sides.position: The ninth of Nisan, reckoned from the end of the mourning for Moses and the return of the spies
The spies' own errand: they returned on the third day and the proclamation followed at once
Three days after the departure had been intimated, since they did not halt at the bank longer than one night

debates.question: Was the pillar of cloud still with them?

sides.position: Removed, since otherwise it would have led them — unless it now hovered over the ark, giving a double guide
Probably still hovering over the ark: till now it went in the middle of the cloudy pillar, and now goes in front

themes: And Joshua rose early in the morning; and they removed from Shittim, and came to Jordan, he and all the children of Israel, and lodged there before they passed over.
And it came to pass after three days, that the officers went through the host;
And they commanded the people, saying, When ye see the ark of the covenant of the Lord your God, and the priests the Levites bearing it, then ye shall remove from your place, and go after it.
Yet there shall be a space between you and it, about two thousand cubits by measure: come not near unto it, that ye may know the way by which ye must go: for ye have not passed this way heretofore.
And Joshua said unto the people, Sanctify yourselves: for to morrow the Lord will do wonders among you.
And Joshua spake unto the priests, saying, Take up the ark of the covenant, and pass over before the people. And they took up the ark of the covenant, and went before the people.

7.pericope_label: This day will I begin to magnify thee: hereby ye shall know

schools.summary: Attend to the construction of the title given to God, since a mistaken exposition has grown from the accents. The genitive depends on the word covenant, and though the punctuators separated the words, they did not thereby put them in apposition or give any support to the exposition that the ark of the covenant is called the ruler of the whole earth. Reject that reading by naming the scholars who gave it. And observe that the description of Jehovah as Lord of the whole earth, which is repeated two verses later, is very appropriately chosen for the purpose of strengthening the people's confidence.

Make the sign reach further than the passage. The power of the miracle extends beyond the entrance of the land, since merely to open a way into hostile territory with no retreat would have been exposure to death, the people destroyed among straits in an unknown region or worn out by hunger and the want of all things. When God restores the river to its course it is as if he stretched forth his hand to rout the inhabitants, so the passage is a presage of the victory to come; and since God does not abandon the work of his hands midway, leaving it maimed and unfinished, learn prudently to combine the acts of divine goodness relating to our salvation, that a happy commencement may keep alive the hope of an equally happy end. But do not let the miracle stand as the ground of faith. When Joshua says the people will know God's presence from it, he indirectly upbraids them with their distrust, since the mere promise ought to have sufficed, and faith not founded solely on that promise must be continually wavering; yet experimental knowledge may act as a secondary support to faith's weakness, for what God promises in word he seals by act. On the title in the next verse, report that some Jewish and Christian interpreters, on the strength of an accent distinguishing the word covenant, read it as calling the ark itself the Lord of all the earth.

Read the verse as assurance given to men apt to be discouraged and to faint at even the appearance of danger. They are to combat idolaters who have nothing to trust in but gods of wood and stone and metal, whereas they are to have the living God in the midst of them, the author of life and being, who can give it or take it away at his pleasure and who by this miracle proved that he had undertaken to guide and defend them. Then set out where the seven nations lay, since the promise names them: the Canaanites chiefly in Phoenicia about Tyre and Sidon; the Hittites in the mountains southward; the Hivites by Ebal and Gerizim and toward Hermon; the Girgashites beyond Jordan; the Jebusites in Jerusalem; the Amorites in the mountainous country near the western part of the Dead Sea; and the Perizzites probably no distinct nation or tribe at all, but villagers scattered through the country in general.

Read the passage as an exchange of honours: God magnifies Joshua so that the people may magnify him, and Joshua turns that honour back by making them know whose God it is — for those that honour God he will honour, and those whom he has advanced should do what they can to exalt him. Note that God spoke to Joshua as he had to Moses from off the mercy-seat, which would make him easy in himself and great among the people; and draw the parallel the passage invites, that as the dividing of the Red Sea convinced Israel God was with Moses in bringing them out, so the dividing of Jordan convinces them he is with Joshua in bringing them in. Add the coincidence of place: it was at the banks of Jordan that God began to magnify Joshua, and at the same place he began to magnify our Lord as Mediator, since John was baptizing at Bethabara, the house of passage. Then ask why the crossing had to be miraculous at all, and answer from what would not have served. God could by a sudden and miraculous frost have congealed the surface so that they might all have gone over upon the ice; but that being a thing sometimes done in that country by the ordinary power of nature, it would not have been such an honour to Israel's God nor such a terror to Israel's enemies. It had therefore to be done in a way with no precedent but the dividing of the Red Sea, that miracle being repeated to show God has the same power to finish the salvation of his people that he had to begin it. And find a second purpose in its form: by dividing the waters and making the dry land appear, God reminded them of what Moses had taught of the work of creation, so that what they saw might assist their belief of what they read.

debates.question: Is the ark itself called 'the Lord of all the earth'?

sides.position: Some Jewish and Christian interpreters read it so, on the strength of an accent distinguishing the word 'covenant'
A mistaken exposition: the genitive depends on 'covenant', and the punctuators' separation gives it no support

debates.question: Why could the crossing not have been made by natural means?

sides.position: A frost congealing the surface is sometimes done in that country by ordinary nature, and would have been no honour to Israel's God nor terror to their enemies
The miracle is a presage of victory over the nations: to open a passage with no retreat would otherwise have been exposure to death

outliers.note: Alone asks why a natural means would not have served and answers from the local climate, that a frost is sometimes had in that country by ordinary nature; and alone notices that God began to magnify Joshua at the same place on Jordan where he afterwards began to magnify our Lord as Mediator, John having baptized at Bethabara.

Alone finds an indirect reproof in the promise of a sign, holding that when Joshua says they will know God's presence from the miracle he upbraids their distrust, the bare promise having been enough — while allowing experimental knowledge as a secondary support to faith's weakness.

Alone locates each of the seven nations named in the promise, from the Canaanites about Tyre and Sidon to the Perizzites, whom he takes to be no distinct nation at all but villagers scattered through the country.

themes: And the Lord said unto Joshua, This day will I begin to magnify thee in the sight of all Israel, that they may know that, as I was with Moses, so I will be with thee.
And thou shalt command the priests that bear the ark of the covenant, saying, When ye are come to the brink of the water of Jordan, ye shall stand still in Jordan.
And Joshua said unto the children of Israel, Come hither, and hear the words of the Lord your God.

And Joshua said, Hereby ye shall know that the living God is among you, and that he will without fail drive out from before you the Canaanites, and the Hittites, and the Hivites, and the Perizzites, and the Girgashites, and the Amorites, and the Jebusites.
Behold, the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth passeth over before you into Jordan.
Now therefore take you twelve men out of the tribes of Israel, out of every tribe a man.

And it shall come to pass, as soon as the soles of the feet of the priests that bear the ark of the Lord, the Lord of all the earth, shall rest in the waters of Jordan, that the waters of Jordan shall be cut off from the waters that come down from above; and they shall stand upon an heap.

14.pericope_label: The waters stood and rose up upon an heap, and the priests stood firm

schools.summary: Confine yourself to the words and render them strictly. The priests stood with the ark of the covenant in the midst of Jordan, that is, in the bed of the river and not merely by the river; and the phrase rendered on dry ground means, literally, with a firm foot, while all Israel went over upon dry ground until the whole people had passed clean over.

Praise the priests before explaining the miracle: their valour in proceeding boldly beyond the bed into the water itself deserved no mean praise, since they might have feared being instantly drowned, and what could they expect on putting in their feet but immediately to find a deep pool in which they would be engulfed? To the general danger was added the special one, that the Jordan had then overflowed, so that the line of the banks and the ford could not be observed and the slime spread far and wide. Then explain the nature of the miracle, for the purpose of removing doubt and preventing profane men from denying the divine interposition by a subtle searching for other causes — and concede what may honestly be conceded. It is not impossible that the flowing of the water might have been restrained for a short time, so that some portion of the channel appeared dry, or that the course might have changed and taken another direction; but it was certainly neither a natural nor a fortuitous event when the waters stood gathered up into a heap. That heap must have been received with fear, leading the Israelites to acknowledge that they were saved in the midst of death, for what was it but a grave in which the whole multitude would have been buried, had the waters resumed their naturally liquid state? Be exact, too, about where the priests began: not at the bank, which was overflowed, but at the water's edge.

Meet head-on the remark often made, that no miracle was needed in crossing Jordan since it is an inconsiderable stream, easily fordable, and but about twenty yards in breadth. The circumstance the sacred historian marks here proves there was a time of year, namely the harvest, when the river overflowed its banks, and another place in Scripture confirms it. Then answer the obvious objection, that the miracle fell about the beginning of April, when rivers are generally lower than in winter: the Jordan rises at the foot of Lebanon, which is covered with snow during the winter months, so the river is low then; but when the summer's sun has melted those snows there is a prodigious increase of waters and the old channel is not capable of containing them. This is why God chose that season, so that a miraculous interposition might be necessary and they should be convinced of his omnipotence. Note too that everything occurred exactly as Joshua had foretold it, which must have greatly increased his credit among the people.

Tell the story plainly, for it is not garnished with the flowers of rhetoric — gold needs not to be painted. Observe that the river was now broader and deeper than at other times of the year, the melting snow on Lebanon making Jordan overflow all his banks at the time of barley-harvest; and that though the opposition given to the salvation of God's people have all imaginable advantages, it is as easy to Omnipotence to divide a river filled to the brim as one ever so narrow. Mark the moment: as soon as ever the priests' feet dipped in the brim of the water, the stream stopped as if a sluice had been let down, the waters above swelling and standing on a heap while those below ran down and left the bottom dry. Note the difference from the earlier deliverance — at the Red Sea the waters were a wall on either hand, here only on the right — and the lesson, that the God of nature can when he pleases turn fluids into solids, and that he sometimes cleaves the earth with rivers and sometimes, as here, cleaves the rivers without earth. Give three reasons for the crossing being made over against Jericho: it was a bold defiance of one of the strongest cities at their first entrance; it encouraged them to venture, having so goodly a city and pleasant a country in view as their own; and it increased the confusion and terror of enemies who were the amazed spectators of this work of wonders. On the priests standing still in the midst, find two purposes: to try their faith, since as they made a bold step when they set the first foot in Jordan, so they made a bold stand when they tarried longest in it; and to encourage the people, that they might go into Canaan fearing no evil in what was for the moment a valley of the shadow of death.

debates.question: Was a miracle needed at all to cross the Jordan?

sides.position: It has often been said not, the stream being fordable and but twenty yards across; but the historian's own aside proves it overflowed its banks in harvest
The flood came just then, when Providence might have restrained it or ordered the crossing at another season — which magnified the power of God

debates.question: How far had the Jordan overflowed?

sides.position: The plain was covered, so that neither the banks nor the ford could be made out and the slime spread far and wide
The original says only that Jordan fills its banks completely, not that it spread beyond them; the Greek version and Luther agree, and the difference has given the infidel a handle

outliers.note: Alone answers the standing objection that the Jordan is too small a stream to need a miracle, explaining from the snows of Lebanon why a river low in winter should be in flood in April, and concluding that God chose that season precisely so that a miraculous interposition should be necessary.

Alone concedes what a naturalistic account might explain — that the flow could have been briefly restrained or the course diverted — in order to locate the miracle precisely in the waters standing gathered into a heap; and alone reads that heap as a grave in which the multitude would have been buried had the waters resumed their liquid state.

Alone notes that at the Red Sea the waters were a wall on either hand and here only on the right, and alone gives three reasons for the crossing being made over against Jericho — defiance of the strongest city, encouragement from the country in view, and terror to the watching enemy.

themes: And it came to pass, when the people removed from their tents, to pass over Jordan, and the priests bearing the ark of the covenant before the people;

And as they that bare the ark were come unto Jordan, and the feet of the priests that bare the ark were dipped in the brim of the water, (for Jordan overfloweth all his banks all the time of harvest,)

That the waters which came down from above stood and rose up upon an heap very far from the city Adam, that is beside Zaretan: and those that came down toward the sea of the plain, even the salt sea, failed, and were cut off: and the people passed over right against Jericho.

And the priests that bare the ark of the covenant of the Lord stood firm on dry ground in the midst of Jordan, and all the Israelites passed over on dry ground, until all the people were passed clean over Jordan.
